source.title: Representation Alignment Rests on Linear Structure
source.authors: Kiril Bangachev; Guy Bresler; Yury Polyanskiy

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; figure text is sometimes flattened, so figure-only pairwise values are not assigned to specific model pairs.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests refinements and qualifications of representation alignment, including dependence on training data, objectives, preprocessing, and similarity metric. It reports evidence about model-pair alignment and cross-model sparse-feature correspondence.
record.gate_note: The paper reports aggregate alignment trends and a matched sparse-feature correlation result; it does not provide extractable individual pairwise values for the large heatmaps. It also discusses dictionary incoherence versus representation dimension, and gives a theoretical account of shared local neighborhoods versus differing global geometry; these are not recorded as empirical alignment rows. Results cited from other papers are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper measures cross-model alignment on 30 representations from LLMs, text embedders, CLIP/SigLIP towers and image models. It reports how alignment changes with sparse versus dense features, centering, KNN neighbourhood size, metric, input word frequency, and model specifications. It also argues for a restated account: a shared sparse object–attribute signal, distorted by model bias and noise, with local but not global geometry shared. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that alignment comes from a shared sparse, linearly encoded object–attribute signal (linking the Linear and Platonic Representation Hypotheses), distorted by model-specific bias (partly removable by centering) and by finite-data noise (higher for rare inputs). Their statistical model implies that local neighbourhoods are shared while global geometry need not be. They read more training data and newer models as moving representations toward the Platonic signal.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than reproducing the original PRH measurement alone, the paper studies sparse-autoencoder features, mean-centering and normalization, word-frequency effects, and model-specification regressions; it compares KNN overlap with other similarity metrics and settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment results vary with feature processing (sparse versus dense and centering/re-normalization), KNN neighborhood size (k=10 versus k=100), similarity metric, and input-word frequency. The text reports centering improvements as consistent across tested datasets and metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: The incoherence of SAE dictionaries (mean absolute off-diagonal inner product) falls with representation dimension, while that of raw embeddings does not (Figure 4, Appendix C.6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-dimensional models learn more nearly orthogonal feature dictionaries, which may explain why measured alignment rises with width.

record.problems: The tested models are up to 4B parameters, which the authors note is below frontier scale. The model-specification results are observational ridge-regression associations and do not establish causality; capability is not directly evaluated. The authors also identify limitations in SAE evaluation, including polysemanticity, feature absorption, non-canonical units, dead neurons, varying top-k activity, and shrinkage concerns.
record.rows_left_out: No individual model-pair heatmap values or the many metric-by-dataset pairwise entries were extracted because the supplied figure text is flattened and does not reliably map values to model pairs. Aggregate textual outcomes and the stated opposing KNN-10/KNN-100 result are retained in r2–r4. Other regression coefficients and the word-frequency regression values are shown in plots but not described numerically in text.

untested.parts: No direct capability measure. The coefficients for parameter count, depth and width are shown only in Figure 7 and not described in text. All models are 4B parameters or fewer.
Image–caption pairs are compared across towers, but not as a function of model quality.
No mapping, stitching or unpaired interchangeability is tested.
Whether matched SAE features share human-interpretable semantics, and whether circuits recur, is not tested.
Plateau, completeness of alignment, and the role of shared training data (as opposed to its quantity) are not tested.

missing.what: The frequency–alignment trend holds for most metrics but not for SVCCA-10. It is weaker for LLM–LLM and text–text pairs, and stronger for larger models within a family.
Specification effects are consistent across metrics, datasets and ridge λ (ordinal consistency of alignment across metrics).
The low alignment of ViT-MAE models with others under dense features is largely removed with sparse features.
Sparse features lower alignment among some same-modality (multimodal image) pairs; KNN-10 gains are small where alignment is already high (LLM–LLM, text embedders).
An SAE dimension ablation (d=8192) shows no qualitative or quantitative difference from d=16384.

record.verdict_notes: Corrections: V7 links are removed from r3, r5, r8 and r9. Training-data quantity is not shared data, and the authors interpret it as noise reduction, which bears on V1. The reader's V7 limits_scope label built on r2–r3 is dropped; that KNN-scale finding belongs to V6. r2 and r3 are set to observed for V6, since the version names dependence on processing and settings.

versions.untested_parts: No direct scaling intervention or sweep links parameter count or measured downstream capability to alignment; the reported training-data and release-year associations are not a direct test of capability.
The paper compares cross-modal representations, but does not test whether paired vision and language representations align more as both models improve.
Different random initializations of the same architecture and shared subspaces across seeds are not tested.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability procedure is tested.
The study tests matching/correlation of SAE sparse features, but does not establish that the matched features have the same human-interpretable semantics or circuits.
The study tests several similarity metrics, KNN settings, centering/normalization, and word-frequency conditions; it does not test out-of-distribution inputs.

Training-data quantity and objective/modality associations are reported, but the study does not establish that these causes explain alignment instead of a common model of reality, nor directly test a plateau or quantify completeness of alignment.

top-k sparse autoencoders; dimension 16384; k=32 for text, 64 for multimodal, 128 for image-only models

rows.measure: Matched sparse-feature correlation minus permutation-null correlation, standardized by the permutation-null standard deviation
rows.baseline: Randomly permuted objects; null mean and standard deviation
rows.value: The difference is on the order of thousands of standard deviations of the permutation null
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation of the permutation null is used for standardization; exact values not stated in the text
rows.note: Aggregate result; the paper says the result strongly rejects the permutation-null hypothesis. It does not report individual pairwise values in the text.
rows.check: Link is correct. Matched SAE-feature correlation exceeds the object-permutation null by thousands of null SDs (Section 3.1, Figures 16–18). Note that feature semantics are not checked, so this shows feature correspondence, not interpretable universal features.

conditions.value: CKA, Unbiased CKA, SVCCA, KNN overlap, and KNN edit distance at tested settings
